title: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
hook: a Sufi's tomb in the Deccan, Muslim rites inside, and a gate that lets everyone in

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hindu-Muslim shared saints found one nearness named in two houses: Kabir's right beside you, and the Qur'an's jugular vein. Today, the week looks back from a gate in the Deccan.

Exam week. A lucky pen, a candle, a grandmother's blessing at the door. In Gulbarga, on the Deccan plateau, some families carry that worry through the gate of a shrine. The air smells of rose petals. Someone lays a cloth over a tomb. A child who's nervous about a test stands holding flowers. The man buried here is a Sufi, remembered by the name Gesu Daraz. The family at the gate isn't Muslim. Nobody stops them, and nobody asks them to be anything other than what they are.
screen: `A LUCKY PEN, A BLESSING.` → `ROSE PETALS AT A GATE.` → `A SUFI'S TOMB.`

segments.voice: The shrine is a dargah: the tomb of a Sufi saint and the place that grows up around it. Sufis are Muslims who walk a path of drawing near to God, often through a chain of teachers. Khwaja Banda Nawaz, called Gesu Daraz, is remembered as a Chishti, one of the Sufi orders. The prayers at the tomb are Muslim prayers, and the saint's yearly day, the urs, is kept by the shrine's Muslim community. And yet the people coming through the gate include Hindus, with flowers, a thread, a bow. What they bring often has a Hindu shape: darshan, seeing a holy one and being seen. Nobody asks them to convert. Nobody turns the tomb into a temple. Now hold up the week. A student on a battlefield who bows, asks and serves. Viveka, the jewel the seeker carries in. Two honest voices on the guru. Kabir's flowers, split in half. Guru and pir, side by side. A nearness two houses name. And this gate: open, with the rites still Muslim.
screen: `A DARGAH: A SUFI'S TOMB.` · `MUSLIM RITES INSIDE.` · `HINDU VISITORS AT THE GATE.` · then, large: `THE GATE STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the people outside your own tradition who have welcomed you somewhere: a home, a table, a doorway. One finger for each. Stay a breath with each face before you move to the next. If you run out of fingers, good. If you only reach one, that one counts too.
Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, a Sufi's tomb in the Deccan: Muslim rites inside, Hindu visitors at the gate.
Something to keep: Hindu-Muslim shared saints, Kabir and the Sufis of the Deccan, taught as history, at a gate that stays open. That's the week.
